stages.title: What is history?
stages.hook: Who lived in your home before you? How could you find out?
explain: History is the story of what happened long ago. It is about real people, real places and real things.
We learn history from clues. Old photos, letters, tools, buildings and stories told by grandparents are all clues. People who study the past look at the clues and ask questions.

example.q: You find an old key in the garden. How can it help you learn history?
steps: Look at the key. Is it rusty? Is it big or small?
Ask: who made it? Who used it? What did it open?
Ask someone older, or look in a book, to find out more.
example.a: The key is a clue about the past.

analogies.home: A box of old photos shows what your family looked like long ago.
analogies.nature: An old tree has rings inside. The rings are clues about how many years it grew.
analogies.city: An old building in town tells you how people built houses long ago.

stages.mnemonic: History is a detective story. The clues are old things and old stories.
terms: The story of what happened in the past.
Something that helps us find out about the past.
The time that has already happened.

misc.wrong: History is only about kings and queens.
misc.right: History is about everyone: farmers, builders, children, cooks and families.

stages.limits: Some things in the past were never written down, so we only know them from objects or from stories told aloud.

trip.prompt: Look at the pictures. Find one old thing and say what it might tell us.

questions.q: What is history?
o: The story of what happened long ago
A song about days that are still to come
A game that is played with cards
questions.why: History tells us about things that happened in the past.

questions.q: Which one is a clue about the past?
o: A picture you draw for tomorrow
A new toy still in a box
questions.why: An old tool was used by people long ago, so it tells us how they lived.

questions.q: Who can tell you stories about the past?
o: Only kings and queens from long ago
Nobody at all can tell them
Only people who teach in schools
questions.why: Older people remember things and can share them as stories.

questions.q: History is about...
questions.why: History is about people everywhere, of every kind.

questions.q: You find a very old clay cup. What is a good question to ask?
o: Who used this cup, and for what?
Can this old cup talk to us?
How many stars are in the sky tonight?
questions.why: Good questions about a clue ask who, what and why.

questions.q: Why do we look at old photos?
o: They show us what the past looked like
They tell us what will happen next
They are always brand new and shiny
They can make rain come down
questions.why: A photo is a clue that shows a moment from the past.

questions.q: A building has stood for a very long time. What can it show us?
o: What we will eat next week
questions.why: Old buildings are clues about the skills and lives of people in the past.

questions.q: Is history only found in books?
o: No. It is also in objects, buildings and stories
Yes. It is only found in books
Yes. It is only on screens
Yes. It is only in schools
questions.why: Clues about the past are in many places, not only in books.

questions.q: Match each clue to what it can show.
questions.why: Each kind of clue tells us about a part of life in the past.

questions.q: Put the steps in order to learn about the past.
questions.why: We find a clue, look at it, ask questions, then share.

panel.q: Why can two people tell the same past story a little differently?
o: They may remember or notice different parts
The past changes again every single day
One of them is always telling lies
A story can never be told two times
panel.why: People see and remember different parts, so we use many clues.

panel.q: Why is it good to use more than one clue?
o: More clues help us be surer
Clues are boring to look at
Clues are too easy to break
panel.why: Several clues that agree make our answer stronger.

panel.q: A tool is found with no name on it. What can we still learn?
o: How it was made and used
The name of the maker for sure
What the maker ate every day
panel.why: We can study the shape and wear, but we cannot know everything.

teach.model: History is the story of what happened long ago. We find it out from clues like old photos, tools and houses. We can also ask older people to tell us their stories.

points.ask: How do we know about it?
Who can tell us about it?

stages.title: Past, present and future
stages.hook: Yesterday, today and tomorrow. Which one can you change?
explain: The past is what has already happened, like yesterday. The present is now. The future is what has not happened yet, like tomorrow.
Words help us know the time. We say 'yesterday' and 'last year' for the past. We say 'now' and 'today' for the present. We say 'tomorrow' and 'next week' for the future.

example.q: Is 'I ate breakfast this morning' past, present or future?
steps: Read the sentence. Did it already happen?
Yes, you ate it. It is finished.
Finished things are in the past.

analogies.home: Dinner you ate last night is past. Dinner you are eating now is present. Dinner for tomorrow is future.
analogies.nature: A seed in the ground is the present. The plant it will become is the future. The seed's parent plant is the past.
analogies.sport: A goal that was scored is past. The kick happening now is present. The next match is future.

stages.mnemonic: Past is behind, present is here, future is ahead.
terms: The time that is happening now.
Time that has not come yet.

misc.wrong: The past is gone, so it does not matter.
misc.right: The past helps us understand today and plan for tomorrow.

stages.limits: People in different places have talked about time in different ways, but every culture has words for before, now and later.

trip.prompt: Look for a clock or a calendar. What does it help us count?

questions.q: Which word is about the past?
questions.why: Yesterday has already happened.

questions.q: Which word is about the future?
questions.why: Tomorrow has not come yet.

questions.q: What is the present?
questions.why: The present is the time that is happening now.

questions.q: 'We will visit the market next week.' When is this?
questions.why: Next week has not happened yet.

questions.q: 'My grandmother was a child long ago.' When is this?
questions.why: Being a child long ago is finished, so it is past.

questions.q: Which can you still change?
questions.why: We cannot change the past, but we can choose what to do next.

questions.q: A photo was taken last summer. It shows...
questions.why: A photo keeps a moment that has already happened.

questions.q: Why do we learn about the past?
o: To understand today and choose well
To forget the things that happened
To make all of time stand still
To skip over the whole future
questions.why: The past helps us understand how things came to be.

questions.q: Match the time word to when it is.
questions.why: Each word points to a time before, during or after now.

questions.q: Put these in order from the past to the future.
questions.why: Time goes from long ago, to now, to later.

panel.q: A seed is planted today. Which is the future?
o: The tall plant it may grow into
The hole that it sits in
The pot it was bought in at the shop
panel.why: The future is what has not happened yet.

panel.q: Why is 'now' always changing?
o: The clock on the wall is broken
All the days are the same
panel.why: Each moment becomes past as the next one arrives.

panel.q: Why might a family keep a diary?
o: So the present can be remembered in the future
So that the future can be turned back into the past
So that time will stop for the family
To make the past much shorter
panel.why: What we write today becomes a record of the past for people later.

teach.model: The past is what already happened, like yesterday. The present is now. The future is what comes next, like tomorrow. We can learn from the past and plan for the future.

stages.title: Timelines and chronological order
stages.hook: How could you line up your birthdays so that the oldest one comes first?
explain: A timeline is a line that shows things in the order they happened. The earliest thing is on the left. The latest is on the right.
Putting things in order is called chronological order. A timeline helps us see what came first, what came next and what came last.

example.q: Put in order: you walk, you crawl, you are born.
steps: Think: what came first? Being born.
Then babies crawl.
Then they walk.

analogies.home: A row of family photos from baby to now makes a timeline.
analogies.nature: A seed, a shoot, a flower: nature has its own timeline.
analogies.music: A song has a first note, a middle and an end, always in order.

stages.mnemonic: Timeline: first on the left, last on the right.
terms: A line that shows events in the order they happened.
In the order that things happened.

misc.wrong: A timeline can be in any order.
misc.right: A timeline must go in the order things happened, from earliest to latest.

stages.limits: Timelines are simple. They show order well, but they do not show why things happened.

trip.prompt: Look at a timeline picture. Which event is first and which is last?

questions.q: What does a timeline show?
o: Events in the order they happened
Only the animals that lived then
What the weather was on one day
questions.why: A timeline puts events in order.

questions.q: On a timeline, where is the earliest event?
questions.why: We read timelines from left to right, earliest first.

questions.q: What does 'chronological order' mean?
o: From the biggest thing to the smallest
From the loudest thing to the quietest
Any order at all that you like
questions.why: Chronological means in time order.

questions.q: Which comes first for a plant?
questions.why: A plant begins as a seed.

questions.q: A timeline has: 'Started school', 'Born', 'Learned to walk'. Which should be last?
questions.why: Being born, then walking, then school: school comes last.

questions.q: Why is a timeline useful?
o: It shows what came first and next
It makes time go by much faster
It can tell us what happens in the future
It helps us to hide the past
questions.why: A timeline helps us see the order of events.

questions.q: Two old tools: one is 100 years old, one is 500 years old. Which is on the left of a timeline?
questions.why: The older tool belongs earlier, so further left.

questions.q: Can a timeline tell us why something happened?
o: Not by itself; it shows order only
Yes, it always tells us why
Yes, if it is drawn in colours
No. It only tells us about the future
questions.why: A timeline shows order, and we need more clues to explain why.

questions.q: Put these in order, earliest first.
questions.why: A person grows through these stages in this order.

questions.q: Match each to its place on a timeline.
questions.why: Order runs from left to right.

panel.q: A boy says: 'My bike came after my trike, but I got the trike when I was older.' What is wrong?
panel.why: What comes after must be later, so the story does not fit.

panel.q: Why do we need dates on a timeline?
panel.why: Dates give the time of each event so we can order it.

panel.q: Which event could not be placed on a timeline of your life?
o: One that has not happened to you yet
Your first day at a new school
Learning how to read a book
panel.why: Only things that happened can be placed in order.

teach.model: A timeline is a line that puts things in the order they happened. The earliest thing goes on the left and the latest on the right. It helps us see what came first and what came last.

points.ask: What does a timeline put in order?
Where do the first and last things go?
What kinds of things go on it?

stages.title: Families and community histories
stages.hook: Does your family have a story that is told again and again? Who tells it?
explain: Every family has a history. It has places they came from, names, songs, foods and stories. A community is a group who live or work together, like a village or a school. It has a history too.
We learn family history by asking questions and listening. Some families tell stories out loud, and some keep photos or write them down. All of these are good ways to remember.

example.q: How can you learn about your grandparent's childhood?
steps: Think of questions: where did you live? What games did you play?
Ask them and listen carefully.
Write or draw what you learn.
example.a: Ask, listen and record the answers.

analogies.home: A family tree shows who is related and how.
analogies.city: A street festival that happens every year tells a town's history.
analogies.farm: A village remembers the year of a great harvest in songs and stories.

terms: The story of your family over time.
A group of people who live or work together.
History told aloud and passed on by speaking.

misc.wrong: Only written things count as history.
misc.right: Spoken stories, songs and photos also keep history.

stages.limits: Memories can change a little as they are retold, so it helps to ask more than one person.

trip.prompt: Find out how people share history by speaking. Who tells the stories?

questions.q: What is a community?
o: A group of people who live or work together
questions.why: A village, a school or a town is a community.

questions.q: What is oral history?
questions.why: Oral means spoken. Families pass stories on aloud.

questions.q: What does a family tree show?
o: Who is in a family and how they are related
questions.why: A family tree maps relatives across generations.

questions.q: How can you learn your family's history?
o: Just guess what might have happened
Never ask anyone anything at all
Wait for the rain to come down
questions.why: Asking and listening is a good way to learn.

questions.q: A town holds a festival every year to remember a long-ago event. What does it do?
o: It stops the past from happening
It hides the town's history away
questions.why: Festivals help communities remember and share their story.

questions.q: Which is a way to keep a family story?
o: Write it, draw it or tell it
Forget it as fast as you can
Hide it in a box for ever
questions.why: Stories can be kept in many ways.

questions.q: Why is it good to ask more than one person about a past event?
o: They are always wrong about it
It is a much faster way to find out
It makes the event happen all over again
questions.why: Different people add different pieces to the story.

questions.q: Why do all families and communities have history?
questions.why: Every group of people has lived through time.

questions.q: Match the way to the story it keeps.
questions.why: Different things keep different parts of the past.

questions.q: Put these steps in order.
questions.why: Prepare, ask, listen, then record.

panel.q: A family moved from one country to another. How can their history stay alive?
o: They tell stories, cook foods and sing songs
They must forget all of it
Only a book can ever keep it
panel.why: Stories, food and songs carry history across places.

panel.q: Why should we listen with respect to older people's stories?
o: They hold knowledge we may not find anywhere else
They are never right about it
It does not matter at all
panel.why: Elders remember things that may not be written anywhere.

panel.q: Which has the longer history?
o: Both a village and a family have history
Only the village has a history
Only the family has a history, not the village
Neither of them has a history
panel.why: Every group has a past, large or small.

teach.model: Every family and every community has a history. We learn it by asking older people and listening to their stories. We can also keep it in photos, songs and drawings.

points.ask: How can we keep it safe?

stages.title: Ancient settlements and everyday life
stages.hook: Long ago, people chose where to build a home. What would you look for: water, food or shelter?
explain: A settlement is a place where people live together. Long ago, many people settled near rivers, because rivers give water for drinking, crops and animals.

In old settlements, people made houses from mud bricks, wood, stone or reeds. They cooked, made pots, wove cloth and traded. Places such as Çatalhöyük in Turkey, Skara Brae in Scotland and Mohenjo-daro in the Indus Valley show how people lived.

example.q: Why is a river a good place for a village?
steps: People need water to drink.
Water helps crops grow.
Rivers also help people travel and carry things.
example.a: Rivers give water, food and ways to travel.

analogies.home: A home needs a roof, a door and a place to cook. So did an ancient house.
analogies.farm: A village near a river could water its fields.
analogies.city: Roads and markets in a town are like paths and trading spots in an ancient settlement.

stages.mnemonic: Water, food, shelter: people settle where they find all three.
terms: A place where people live together.
Swapping or selling things with others.
A brick made from mud dried in the sun.

misc.wrong: Long ago, everyone lived in caves.
misc.right: People lived in many kinds of homes, such as huts, mud-brick houses and stone houses.

stages.limits: We learn about daily life from objects and ruins, so some details are guesses.

trip.prompt: Look at the stone houses. What did the people use in their rooms?

questions.q: What is a settlement?
o: A place where people live together
questions.why: A settlement is a village or town where people live.

questions.q: Why did people often settle near rivers?
questions.why: Rivers give water to drink and to grow crops.

questions.q: What is a mud brick?
o: A brick made from mud dried in the sun
A brick made of pure shining gold
A brick made out of ice
A brick that floats on water
questions.why: Mud bricks were a common building material in warm lands.

questions.q: Which is a clue that people lived in a place long ago?
o: Fresh flowers growing in a pot
A shop that has just opened
questions.why: Pots and walls are left behind by people long ago.

questions.q: People found good soil and water. What would they likely do?
o: Leave at once and never come back
Build a boat and nothing else
questions.why: Soil and water make farming and living possible.

questions.q: Where is Skara Brae?
questions.why: Skara Brae is a stone-age village in Scotland.

questions.q: Which people made pots?
questions.why: Pot-making was invented and used in many places.

questions.q: Why did people trade?
o: To get things they could not make themselves
To hide things away from others
Because they were told to be very loud
questions.why: Trade lets people get things from others.

questions.q: Match the place to where it is.
questions.why: These settlements are in Europe, western Asia and South Asia.

questions.q: Put these in order: how a village begins.
questions.why: People find a good place, build, farm and later trade.

panel.q: A river dried up near a village. What might the people do?
panel.why: Without water people have to move or find new water.

panel.q: Why did people build homes from the things near them?
o: They were close and easy to use
panel.why: Local materials were easiest to find.

panel.q: Why do ruins of old houses help us?
o: They show us nothing at all
They show what the weather will be
panel.why: Ruins are clues about daily life.

teach.model: A settlement is a place where people live together. Long ago many people settled near rivers because they needed water. They built houses from mud, wood or stone, grew food and traded.

stages.title: Early farming and human inventions
stages.hook: Before farms, people searched for food every day. What changed when they could grow it?
explain: For most of human history, people hunted animals and gathered plants. Then, in different places at different times, people began to grow crops and keep animals. This is called farming.

Farming began in many parts of the world. People grew wheat and barley in West Asia, rice in China, maize in Mexico, potatoes in the Andes, and millet and sorghum in Africa. Farming let people stay in one place.
People also invented tools to help: the plough, pots to store food, the wheel and the loom for weaving.

example.q: Why did farming let people build villages?
steps: Crops grow in one place.
People must stay to water and care for them.
Staying together makes a village.
example.a: Crops keep people in one place.

analogies.home: A small garden at home gives food without a long walk.
analogies.farm: A farmer saves some seeds to plant next year.
analogies.nature: A seed in the soil grows into food when it has sun and rain.

stages.mnemonic: Seed, sun, soil: farming starts with S-S-S.
terms: Growing plants and keeping animals for food.
A new tool or idea that someone makes.
A plant that people grow for food.

misc.wrong: Farming began in only one place.
misc.right: People started farming in several parts of the world, on their own.

stages.limits: Scholars do not agree on exactly why farming began, and dates differ by place.

trip.prompt: Find a map of where different crops were first grown.

questions.q: What is farming?
o: Growing plants and keeping animals for food
questions.why: Farming means growing crops and keeping animals.

questions.q: Which crop was first grown in Mexico?
questions.why: Maize (corn) was first grown in Mexico.

questions.q: Which crop was first grown in China?
questions.why: Rice was grown in China from very early times.

questions.q: Why did farming help villages grow?
o: People could not eat their food
Crops walked away on their own
People had no tools at all to use
questions.why: Growing food in one place meant people lived there.

questions.q: What did people use pots for?
o: To play loud drums and nothing else
To fly up into the sky
questions.why: Pots kept grain and water safe.

questions.q: Which invention helped people carry heavy things?
questions.why: Wheels made it easier to move loads.

questions.q: A farmer saves seeds from the best plants. Why?
o: To hide them from birds all year
questions.why: Saved seeds grow into next year's crop.

questions.q: Farming began in many places. What does this show?
o: People in different places had similar ideas
One person copied what everyone else did
Farming is very easy to learn
It all happened in only one day
questions.why: Different peoples found farming on their own.

questions.q: Match the crop to the place it was first grown.
questions.why: Different crops came from different parts of the world.

questions.q: Put these in order for growing food.
questions.why: Seeds are planted, watered, grow, then are harvested.

panel.q: Why might farming make a better store of food than hunting?
o: You can save grain for later
Animals are always gone by winter
panel.why: Stored grain gives food through the year.

panel.q: A village has more food than it needs. What might happen?
o: Some people can do other jobs
panel.why: Extra food lets some people make pots, tools and more.

panel.q: Why were new tools important to farmers?
o: They made the crops feel sad
panel.why: Tools like the plough made work faster.

teach.model: Long ago people hunted and gathered food. Then they learned to grow crops and keep animals. Farming started in many places, and it let people stay in one place and build villages.

points.ask: What did people learn to do?

stages.title: Archaeological discoveries
stages.hook: If you dig in the ground and find a pot, what can it tell you?
explain: An archaeologist is someone who studies the past by digging carefully and looking at things people left behind. These things are called artefacts. Pots, tools, jewellery and buildings are artefacts.

Some famous finds help us a lot. The Rosetta Stone, found in Egypt in 1799, had the same words in three kinds of writing, which helped people read Egyptian hieroglyphs. The Terracotta Army in China was found in 1974 by farmers digging a well.

example.q: Why do archaeologists dig slowly and carefully?
steps: Old things can break easily.
Where things lie is a clue.
Careful work keeps the clues safe.
example.a: So they do not break or lose clues.

analogies.home: Finding an old toy under a bed tells you what children played with.
analogies.nature: Layers of soil are like pages in a book. Deeper ones are older.
analogies.sea: Divers find old ships on the sea floor that show how people travelled.

terms: A person who studies the past by digging and examining old things.
An object made by people long ago.

misc.right: They look for clues about how people lived, and the clues can be everyday things.

stages.limits: Objects only survive in some conditions, so the record of the past has gaps.

trip.prompt: Look at the three kinds of writing. Why did that help?

questions.q: What does an archaeologist do?
o: Studies the past by digging and examining old things
Predicts the weather for the week
questions.why: Archaeologists learn from things people left behind.

questions.q: What is an artefact?
o: An object made by people long ago
A rock that formed all on its own
A kind of tree in the woods
questions.why: Artefacts are things people made or used.

questions.q: What helped people read Egyptian hieroglyphs?
questions.why: It had the same text in three writing systems.

questions.q: Who found the Terracotta Army in China?
questions.why: In 1974 farmers found it while digging a well.

questions.q: A digger finds a broken pot. What should be done?
o: Handle it gently and note where it was
Smash it into even more pieces
Ignore it and just walk on
questions.why: Where and how a pot lies is part of the clue.

questions.q: Which is an artefact?
o: A stone tool made by hand
A river that flows to the sea
A white cloud in the sky
questions.why: Only the tool was made by people.

questions.q: Deeper layers of earth are usually...
questions.why: New layers settle on top of old ones.

questions.q: Why do archaeologists record where each find lies?
o: Position gives clues about use and age
To make a map just for fun
So that they can lose it again
To make a lot of noise
questions.why: Context helps explain what the object was for.

questions.q: Match the find to what it helps us learn.
questions.why: Each artefact tells a part of daily life.

questions.q: Put these in order, from first to last.
questions.why: Archaeology moves from finding a place to sharing results.

panel.q: Why are objects from poor and rich homes both useful?
o: Together they show all of daily life
Only the things from rich homes matter
Only the things from poor homes matter
panel.why: All kinds of people were part of the past.

panel.q: Why might some things be missing from a dig?
o: Cloth and wood rot, while stone and pots last
They were never there at all
panel.why: Some materials survive far better than others.

panel.q: Why should finds belong to everyone's heritage?
o: They tell the story of all people
They are only for one person to own
They are just toys to play with
panel.why: The past is shared by people everywhere.

teach.model: An archaeologist digs carefully to find things people left behind long ago. These are called artefacts. They are clues that tell us how people lived.

points.ask: What do the finds tell us?

stages.title: Famous historical monuments
stages.hook: Some buildings and statues have stood for hundreds or thousands of years. Why did people build them?
explain: A monument is a building or structure made to remember something or someone. People around the world built monuments for many reasons: to honour rulers, to worship, to mark the seasons or to remember the dead.

Some famous monuments are the Great Pyramid of Giza in Egypt, the Great Wall in China, Machu Picchu in Peru, Angkor Wat in Cambodia, Great Zimbabwe, Stonehenge in England, Petra in Jordan and the stone statues of Rapa Nui.

example.q: Why do monuments survive for a long time?
steps: Many are built from stone.
Stone lasts longer than wood.
People who care for them keep them standing.

analogies.home: A family keeps a special photo on the wall to remember something.
analogies.city: A statue in a town square helps people remember an event.
analogies.nature: A big old tree can mark a meeting place for a village.

terms: A structure built to remember a person, event or belief.
What is left of old buildings.
Things from the past that we keep for the future.

misc.wrong: Only one part of the world built great monuments.
misc.right: People on every inhabited continent built great monuments.

stages.limits: For some monuments, such as Stonehenge or the Rapa Nui statues, scholars still debate exactly why and how they were made.

trip.prompt: Look at the stone walls. Why was stone a good choice?

questions.q: What is a monument?
o: A structure built to remember something
questions.why: Monuments help people remember.

questions.q: Where is the Great Pyramid of Giza?
questions.why: The Great Pyramid is in Egypt.

questions.q: Where is Machu Picchu?
questions.why: Machu Picchu is in the Andes in Peru.

questions.q: Where is Angkor Wat?
questions.why: Angkor Wat is in Cambodia.

questions.q: Where is the Great Wall?
questions.why: The Great Wall is in China.

questions.q: Why do many old buildings still stand?
o: Made from strong stone and cared for
questions.why: Stone lasts, and care keeps buildings from falling.

questions.q: A town wants to protect its old tower. What should it do?
o: Look after it and teach people about it
questions.why: Heritage is kept by care and sharing knowledge.

questions.q: What can monuments in many countries show us?
o: Only one group was clever enough
Nothing at all about the past
questions.why: Great building happened all over the world.

questions.q: Match the monument to its country.
questions.why: Monuments are found on many continents.

questions.q: Put these steps in order for a new monument.
questions.why: Plans come first, then materials, building and visiting.

panel.q: Why do some people not agree on why Stonehenge was built?
panel.why: Without writing, we must guess from clues.

panel.q: Why is it important not to climb or damage old monuments?
o: They break easily and belong to everyone
panel.why: Damage cannot be undone, and monuments are shared heritage.

panel.q: Which statement is fair?
o: Great monuments were built on many continents
Only one continent ever built monuments
All monuments are the very same
panel.why: No one place has a monopoly on great building.

teach.model: A monument is a building made to remember something. People all over the world built them, like the pyramids in Egypt and Machu Picchu in Peru. They are made of strong stone so they can last, and we keep them safe.

stages.title: Introduction to the world's continents and cultures
stages.hook: The world has seven big pieces of land. Can you name them?
explain: The seven continents are Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia (with Oceania), Europe, North America and South America. People live on every continent except Antarctica, where only scientists stay for a time.
Each place has its own cultures: foods, music, clothes, stories and ways to celebrate. Cultures are different, and none is better than another. History belongs to people everywhere.

example.q: How many continents are there, and where do people live permanently?
steps: Count: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia/Oceania, Europe, North America, South America.
That is 7.
Antarctica has no permanent home for people, so people live on the other 6.

analogies.home: A big family has many people who are different but all belong.
analogies.music: An orchestra has many instruments. Each sounds different and they make music together.
analogies.nature: A garden has many flowers. Each looks different and all are lovely.

stages.mnemonic: Seven continents, many cultures, one world.
terms: One of the world's very large pieces of land.
The way a group of people live: food, music, stories and customs.
The icy continent at the South Pole, with no permanent population.

misc.wrong: One way of life is better than all others.
misc.right: Cultures are different, and each has its own history and value.

stages.limits: Different countries teach different counts of continents (for example, five or six), so the number depends on how they are grouped.

trip.prompt: Find a world map. Point to each continent and say one thing you know about it.

questions.q: How many continents are in the list taught in this game?
questions.why: We count seven: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia/Oceania, Europe, North America and South America.

questions.q: Which continent is very icy and has no permanent home for people?
questions.why: Only scientists stay in Antarctica for a time.

questions.q: What is culture?
o: Food, music, stories and ways of life
questions.why: Culture is how a group of people live and celebrate.

questions.q: Which is the biggest continent?
questions.why: Asia is the largest by area.

questions.q: Which two continents are in the Americas?
questions.why: The Americas are the two continents of the West.

questions.q: A friend from another country eats different food from you. What is the best thing to say?
questions.why: Cultures are different, and curiosity shows respect.

questions.q: Why is Antarctica special for science?
o: Scientists study ice and animals there
questions.why: Antarctica is a place for science and exploration.

questions.q: What is true about all cultures?
o: Each has its own history and value
Only some of them have a history
Only the biggest ones really count
Some of them are better than others
questions.why: Every culture has a past and deserves respect.

questions.q: Match the people to the continent.
questions.why: Great early peoples lived on every continent.

questions.q: Put these from the smallest group to the biggest.
questions.why: A family is in a village, in a country, on a continent.

panel.q: Why might a map in one country put that country in the middle?
o: Mapmakers often choose their own place as the centre
panel.why: Where the centre is placed is a choice, not a ranking.

panel.q: Why does it help to learn history from many continents?
o: It gives a fuller, fairer picture
It is much shorter to learn
It is a lot easier to learn
It hides some of the facts
panel.why: Every place added to the story makes it more complete.

panel.q: Why do people live on six continents but not in Antarctica permanently?
o: It is extremely cold and has little food
It has far too many people there
It is much too hot there
It has no ice at all
panel.why: Antarctica is extremely cold, so no permanent homes.

teach.model: The world has seven continents. People live on all of them except Antarctica, where only scientists stay. Each place has its own cultures, such as food, music and stories, and none is better than another.
